dataset.what_one_row_represents: One row in the captions file = one closed-caption line of Ali Wong's Baby Cobra, with start/stop time and a manually measured laughter duration. One row in the topics file = one annotated topic in the routine's hierarchical structure (level 1-6).
dataset.time_range: 2016 (Baby Cobra was filmed Sep 2015, released May 2016 on Netflix); the dataset's internal timeline is the special's runtime, 0:28-58:55.
dataset.geographic_scope: Filmed at the Neptune Theater, Seattle

ana_01.label: Audience laughs for one-fifth of the hour
ana_01.content: Across the 58:27 of stage time covered by the captions, 727 seconds — 20.7% — were spent in audible audience laughter. That's roughly 12 minutes of an hour-long set where the audience, not the comic, is making the noise. Of 925 caption lines, 38.1% (352) carry a non-zero laughter value; the remaining 573 are setups, transitions, or beats with no measurable laugh. When laughter does happen, the median duration is 1.5 seconds and the mean is 2.07 seconds — short reactions are the rule, big ones the exception.

Total set duration (first caption to last): 3507 s
Laughter share of stage time: 20.7%
Laugh-bearing captions: 352 of 925 (38.1%)
Mean laugh duration when present: 2.07 s
Median laugh duration when present: 1.50 s

ana_02.label: The single biggest laugh — the climax line
ana_02.content: Exactly one caption in the entire hour is tagged with a 10-second laugh: 'Colonize the colonizer!' at 11:48, in the topic group '166-hooking up'. Nothing else matches it. The next-largest laugh, 9.5 seconds, comes 38 minutes later ('That's right. 'Cause I don't wanna work anymore' at 50:11, in the conception bit). The 10-second moment is the unique top of the distribution — and it sits early, only 20% of the way through the hour, inside the long marriage chapter rather than the pregnancy chapter most people associate with the special.

ana_03.label: The shape of laughter: long tail
ana_03.content: The distribution of laugh durations is sharply long-tailed. 573 of 925 captions get no laugh at all. Among lines that do trigger laughter, most are short — 41 sit at 0.5s, 47 at 1.0s, 34 at 1.5s. As you move out into the longer durations the counts collapse: only 28 captions hit 5 seconds or more, only 11 reach 7 seconds, only 4 reach 8 seconds, and exactly one reaches 10 seconds. Comedy on this evidence is not a steady stream of equally funny moments — it is a baseline of small smiles punctuated by a handful of rare detonations.

data_table.description: Histogram of laugh durations across all 925 caption lines

ana_04.label: Laughter by minute — where the hour peaks
ana_04.content: Aggregated minute by minute, the laughter profile of Baby Cobra is uneven but rarely silent. The peak is minute 11, with 21.8 seconds of laughter packed into 60 seconds of stage time — that's the minute that contains the climax line at 11:48. Other strong minutes are 8 (21.0s, the 'trap men' bit), 13 (20.5s, the 'racist together' beat that follows the climax), 33 (19.5s, control / boss), and 37 (20.2s, paintball / Vietnam vet). The quietest non-zero minute is 3.75 seconds. Minute 59 registers zero — that's the closing 'thank you' tail of the special.

calculation.output:
Peak minute: 11 (21.8 s of laughter)
Quietest non-zero minute: 3.75

ana_05.label: Topic ranking: which bits earned the most laughter
ana_05.content: Aggregating the per-caption laughter to the 120 topic groups in the captions file, the bits that got the most total laughter are short, punchy ones: 'hooking up' tops the list at 20.5s of laughter packed into just 35 seconds of stage time (a 0.59 laugh-per-second rate, the highest among long-running bits). 'Bad drivers' (19.8s in 81s on stage) comes second by total but at a much slower rate (0.24/s). The conception bit gets only 24 seconds of stage time but produces 15.2 seconds of laughter — a 0.64/s density, denser even than the hooking-up climax. Twenty bits got zero measured laughter; these are mostly setup or connective topics that pay off later.

ana_06.label: Topic structure: a six-level nest
ana_06.content: Wong's set is unusually deep structurally. The annotators recorded 131 topics arranged across 6 nesting levels — 10 at the top, 21 at level 2, 43 at level 3 (the most populated level), 31 at level 4, 19 at level 5, and 7 at level 6. Most stand-up sets are flat lists of bits; this one branches like a tree, with sub-topics sprouting from sub-topics. Level 3 is the workhorse — that's where most of the actual content lives. Levels 4-6 are deep digressions that, structurally, are children of children of children of one of the ten top-level chapters.

Level 2: 21 topics
Level 3: 43 topics
Level 4: 31 topics
Level 5: 19 topics
Level 6: 7 topics
Max depth: 6

ana_07.label: Deeper bits get bigger laughs
ana_07.content: When you bucket every caption by the nesting level of the topic it lives in, average laughter rises with depth — and so do the maximums. Level-1 captions average 0.57s of laughter; level 4 averages 0.90s and contains the only 10-second laugh in the set. Levels 5 and 6 average 0.97s and 0.87s. Level 1 and 2 captions are mostly chapter introductions ('let's talk about marriage', 'let's talk about pregnancy') that exist to set up later bits, not to be funny themselves. The further Wong burrows down a digression, the harder the audience laughs at what she finds. This is the dataset's clearest endorsement of The Pudding's structural argument: payoff tracks depth.

ana_08.label: Three callbacks — and they reach back further than you'd expect
ana_08.content: The topics CSV records exactly three explicit callbacks. The shortest reach-back is still 12 minutes 24 seconds; the longest is 46 minutes 11 seconds. The first ('When I pee, I need to see ten gallons of bleach' → hippies routine, fired at 49:43) reaches back 33 minutes. The second ('blaming mom' → 'told my mom from a third world country', fired at 50:57) reaches back 46 minutes — across nearly the entire special. The third (the 'wet' callback at 56:48 referencing a 'wet' beat at 44:24) reaches back 12 minutes. Distance between setup and callback is enormous: in two of three cases the seed was planted in the first ten minutes of the show and harvested in the last ten.

ana_09.label: Anatomy of the climax: the line lands because of what came before
ana_09.content: Reading the 30 caption lines around the 11:48 climax shows the structural staircase. The setup begins at 11:24 with a 1.0-second laugh ('when a white dude eats my pussy'), grows to 3.0s at 11:31 ('absorbing all of that privilege'), pauses, then jumps to 4.0s at 11:41 ('I could just crush your head at any moment, white man!'). The 10-second peak at 11:48 ('Colonize the colonizer!') only works because the audience has spent the previous 24 seconds tracking the layered conceit — sex as power, power as colonial reversal, the white man as the colonized. Ninety seconds of stage time delivered 39.8 seconds of laughter — twice the show's average density.

ana_10.label: Marriage runs longer — but pregnancy laughs harder
ana_10.content: The five distinct level-1 chapters, in order: intro (0:28-0:49), getting older (0:49-6:50, 83.8s of laughter, 23% of chapter time), marriage (6:55-37:35, by far the longest at 30 minutes 40 seconds, 404s of laughter), paintball (37:38-37:48, a 10-second mini-chapter that scores 8.5s of laugh — 85% of the chapter is laughter), pregnancy (37:57-57:17, 19m 20s, 211s of laughter), and the conclusion. Marriage is the spine of the special — almost half the runtime. Pregnancy is a third of the runtime but earns the second-highest cumulative laughter. The closing two minutes carry zero laugh; that's Wong winding down.

ana_11.label: Motif frequency: what the show is actually about
ana_11.content: Counting how often specific words and phrases recur across the 925 captions is a different kind of structural map — it shows the running threads. 'Asian / Korean / Japanese / Vietnamese' appears in 25 captions, 'husband' in 21, 'mom / mother' in 15, 'money / dollars' in 10, 'HPV' in 8 (clustered in a single bit), 'trap' in 8 (the 'trapping a man' running metaphor). 'Colonize / white guy / white people' appears in just 4 captions — a sparse motif that nevertheless contains the climax. The recurring words trace the show's themes: Asianness, marriage, money, the body. The climax line is dense, not frequent.

caveats.content: Laughter durations are hand-measured by The Pudding annotators in coarse half-second steps, so absolute small-number differences (e.g. 0.5s vs 1.0s) should not be over-interpreted. The headline patterns — the unique 10-second peak, the long-tailed distribution, the depth-versus-laughter trend — are robust to this measurement granularity.

Laughter is contagious and lagged: the seconds tagged to a caption are partly a reaction to that line and partly tail-off from the previous beat. We treat per-caption durations as a directional signal rather than a precise per-line measurement.

The level-1 chapters list shows the same group label twice for marriage, pregnancy, getting-older, and conclusion because the topics CSV uses level-1 rows both to open and to close a chapter. We aggregated to one row per (group, start, end) tuple for the data table.
